title: CloudFront + S3: can a website run from a private bucket?
content:
Here’s a common way to put a frontend (React, Vue, a static Next.js export…) on AWS: build it into a dist/ folder, upload that to Amazon S3, turn on Static website hosting, turn off Block Public Access, and add a bucket policy that lets "Principal": "*" read the objects.
The site works right away. Then a couple of questions come up:
Anyone can call the bucket URL directly and skip the CDN, the WAF and the HTTPS on your real domain. Is that okay? Is there a way to keep the bucket fully private and still have the website work for users? The usual answer is to put Amazon CloudFront in front and use Origin Access Control (OAC). But how does OAC work, and why do so many people get 403 AccessDenied right after turning it on?
1. What is OAC? Origin Access Control lets CloudFront send authenticated requests to an S3 origin. With OAC set to Sign requests (recommended), CloudFront signs every request it sends to S3 and always uses HTTPS between CloudFront and S3 [1].
On the S3 side, the bucket policy only lets the service principal cloudfront.amazonaws.com read objects, with a condition that AWS:SourceArn matches the ARN of your distribution:
"Principal": { "Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket/*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::111122223333:distribution/E2ABC..." } } What you get:
Users coming through the CloudFront domain → allowed. Someone calling the S3 URL directly → 403 AccessDenied. A different CloudFront distribution → also denied, because the SourceArn doesn’t match. The bucket can keep Block Public Access: ON and doesn’t need any public permissions.
2. How is OAC different from OAI? CloudFront used to use Origin Access Identity (OAI). AWS now calls OAI legacy and recommends OAC, because OAC supports [1]:
Every S3 bucket in every AWS Region, including opt-in Regions launched after December 2022. Objects encrypted with SSE-KMS. Dynamic requests such as PUT and DELETE to S3. If you’re on OAI today, you can move over step by step: update the bucket policy to allow both OAI and OAC, switch the distribution to OAC, wait for the deploy to finish, and only then remove the OAI statement. CloudFront keeps access to the bucket the whole time.
3. Common mistake #1: using the S3 website endpoint as the origin S3 has two kinds of endpoint, and picking the wrong one is the most common mistake:
REST endpoint: your-bucket.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com Website endpoint: your-bucket.s3-website-<region>.amazonaws.com If the origin is the website endpoint, CloudFront has to treat it as a custom origin, and then you can’t use OAC (or OAI) [1]. The website endpoint only serves public content.
For a private bucket with OAC, the origin has to be the REST endpoint, and you can turn Static website hosting off on the bucket.
4. Common mistake #2: refreshing an SPA sub-page gives 403 After moving to the REST endpoint with OAC, the home page works, but when a user refreshes on /dashboard they get a 403 instead of the page.
The reason: there’s no object called dashboard in the bucket. Because CloudFront doesn’t have s3:ListBucket, S3 returns 403 AccessDenied instead of 404 for an object that doesn’t exist [3]. That’s sensible from a security point of view (it doesn’t reveal which objects exist), but it means the client-side router never gets a chance to run.
Two common fixes:
For an SPA: set up a Custom error response on the distribution that maps 403 (and 404) → /index.html with response code 200 [4]. For a static site with many folders (docs, blogs): the Default root object only applies to the root URL, so a request for a sub-folder like /docs/ doesn’t return index.html on its own [5]. A CloudFront Function on viewer request can rewrite /docs/ to /docs/index.html. Note: mapping 403 → index.html for the whole distribution also hides real 403 errors (a missing KMS permission, for example). When debugging, check the CloudFront logs or turn the error response off for a while to see the real error.
5. Common mistake #3: SSE-KMS objects are still denied If the bucket uses SSE-KMS with a customer managed key, the bucket policy alone isn’t enough. CloudFront also needs permission to use the KMS key to decrypt objects.
Add a statement to the key policy for the service principal cloudfront.amazonaws.com with kms:Decrypt (plus kms:Encrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey* if you upload through CloudFront), with an AWS:SourceArn condition for your distribution [1].
Without it, the symptom is still a 403. And if you already set up the error response from section 04, you may only see index.html and have no idea why the real file won’t load.
6. Deploying a new version: cache and invalidation With CloudFront in front, content is cached at the edge. Uploading a new build to S3 doesn’t mean users see it right away.
A common approach:
Files with a hash in the name (main.3f9a1c.js, style.8b2e.css): cache for a long time, for example Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable. index.html: short cache or no-cache, so the browser always gets the version that points to the new files. After a deploy, invalidating /index.html is enough, because the hashed files already have new names. On cost: the first 1,000 invalidation paths each month (across the whole account) are free, and after that you pay per path. A wildcard path like /* counts as one path [6]. So you invalidate selectively mainly to avoid wiping the whole cache and sending every request back to the origin right after each deploy; the money is usually small.
7. Checklist before going to production Is the origin the S3 REST endpoint and not the website endpoint? Is Block Public Access on, with a bucket policy that only allows cloudfront.amazonaws.com with the right distribution in AWS:SourceArn? Is OAC set to Sign requests (recommended)? If you use SSE-KMS, does the key policy let the distribution decrypt? Is the viewer protocol policy Redirect HTTP to HTTPS or HTTPS only? Does the SPA have an error response, and does a multi-folder site have a way to rewrite to index.html? Is the caching plan for hashed files and index.html clear? Conclusion S3 static website hosting is the fastest way to get a frontend onto AWS, but it forces the bucket to be public.
CloudFront with OAC splits the roles cleanly. CloudFront is the only way in, with HTTPS, caching and (optionally) WAF. S3 is just private storage that accepts requests signed by the right distribution.
Most problems when moving to OAC come from the details around it: the wrong endpoint, 403 instead of 404, KMS permissions and caching. Once you know these, a website runs fine from a private bucket.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: My Lambda times out after I put it in a VPC: where did the request go?
content:
This one comes up all the time in serverless work.
An order-processing Lambda needs to read data from Amazon RDS in a private subnet. To reach the database, the Lambda gets attached to the VPC. The RDS connection works.
But right away, things that used to work break:
Calling the external payment gateway API → hangs. Getting a password from AWS Secrets Manager → hangs. Sending a message to Amazon SQS → hangs. The logs show no 403 and no DNS error. Just one line:
Task timed out after 3.01 seconds The first instinct is usually to raise the timeout, raise the memory, or move the Lambda to a public subnet so it “has internet”. The last one sounds reasonable but fixes nothing.
1. Without a VPC, Lambda already has internet Every Lambda function runs inside a VPC that Lambda itself owns and manages, which customers can’t see. By default, the function can reach the internet [1].
When you add a VPC configuration, Lambda creates a Hyperplane ENI in the subnet and security group you pick. From then on, the function can only reach what your VPC allows, unless that VPC has a route to the internet [1].
In other words, once you attach a VPC, the way out is yours to manage.
A few things to know when attaching a VPC:
The execution role needs permission to create and manage ENIs, which the managed policy AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole includes [1]. A new function stays in the Pending state and can’t be invoked until the Hyperplane ENI is ready, which can take a few minutes [1]. Functions that share the same subnet and security group combination can share an ENI. 2. Why does it still time out in a public subnet? With EC2, putting an instance in a public subnet and giving it a public IP gets it onto the internet. Many people assume the same works for Lambda.
But the Lambda docs say clearly that connecting a function to a public subnet doesn’t give it internet access or a public IP [1]. The Hyperplane ENI only has a private IP, so even with a 0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway route in the route table, the request can’t get out.
What AWS recommends [2]:
Put the Lambda in a private subnet. Create a NAT Gateway in a public subnet (with an Elastic IP). Private subnet route table: 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway. Public subnet route table: 0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway. The Lambda’s security group allows outbound traffic. For IPv6 on a dual-stack subnet, the private subnet also needs a ::/0 → Egress-only Internet Gateway route [2].
3. Not every destination needs to go through NAT With NAT in place, everything works again. But now every request, including calls to S3, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager and SQS, goes the long way through the NAT Gateway, which charges per hour and per GB processed.
It’s better to split by destination:
External APIs on the internet (payment, SMS, webhooks…) → NAT Gateway. If the destination is outside AWS, there’s no other way.
Amazon S3 and DynamoDB in the same Region → Gateway Endpoint. A route for the service’s prefix list is added to the route table, traffic goes straight to the service without NAT, and Gateway Endpoints cost nothing extra [3].
Other AWS services (Secrets Manager, SQS, STS, KMS, CloudWatch Logs…) → Interface Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink). The endpoint creates an ENI with a private IP in your subnet and is charged per hour and per GB processed [4].
Interface Endpoints don’t need any extra routes. With Private DNS on, the service’s default hostname (for example secretsmanager.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com) resolves to the endpoint’s private IP, so code using the AWS SDK doesn’t need any changes [4].
4. The Interface Endpoint exists but it still times out? It’s also common to create the endpoint and still have the SDK hang. Check these in order:
VPC DNS: to use private DNS, the VPC needs both DNS hostnames and DNS resolution turned on [4]. Otherwise the service hostname still resolves to a public IP and the request goes looking for the internet again. Private DNS name on the endpoint: for services other than S3 it’s on by default, and AWS recommends leaving it on [4]. The endpoint’s security group: it has to allow inbound HTTPS (443) from the caller, here the Lambda’s security group [4]. If you don’t pick one, the endpoint gets the VPC’s default security group. The subnet’s Network ACL must not block traffic between the Lambda and the endpoint’s ENI [4]. Endpoint subnets: you can pick one subnet per AZ. Create the endpoint in the AZs where the Lambda runs. A quick debugging trick: write a test Lambda in the same subnet and security group and do a DNS lookup on the service hostname. A 10.x.x.x result means private DNS works. A public IP means you should go back and check the VPC and endpoint DNS settings.
5. Does the Lambda really need a VPC? It’s worth asking this before any of the steps above. A Lambda only needs a VPC when it has to reach resources inside one: RDS, ElastiCache, EC2, internal services behind an internal load balancer…
If the function only calls S3, DynamoDB, SQS, Secrets Manager and external APIs, leaving it out of the VPC is usually simplest: internet by default, no NAT, no endpoints, no ENIs to worry about.
If only a small part of the logic needs the VPC, consider splitting it into two functions: one inside the VPC that only talks to the database, and one outside that handles the external API calls.
6. Checklist for putting Lambda in a VPC Does the function really need to reach resources inside the VPC? Is the Lambda in private subnets across at least 2 AZs? If it needs the internet: a NAT Gateway in a public subnet, and a 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT route in the private subnet’s route table? Do S3 and DynamoDB have Gateway Endpoints so they skip the NAT? Do other AWS services have Interface Endpoints, or is going through NAT acceptable? Does the VPC have DNS hostnames and DNS resolution on, and does the endpoint’s SG allow 443 from the Lambda’s SG? Can the execution role create ENIs (AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole or an equivalent policy)? Conclusion A “Task timed out” right after attaching a VPC is rarely a code bug or a lack of resources. Most of the time, the request just can’t find a way out.
Once a Lambda is in a VPC, each destination needs its own path: the internet through a NAT Gateway, S3 and DynamoDB through a Gateway Endpoint, other AWS services through an Interface Endpoint.
Knowing where each request goes makes timeouts faster to fix, and keeps traffic to AWS services from taking the long way through NAT for no reason.

IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance weather data collection and analysis. It supports up to 5 weather stations, with potential scalability to 10-15, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge devices with ESP32 sensors to transmit data via MQTT. The platform leverages AWS Serverless services to deliver real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and cost efficiency, with access restricted to 5 lab members via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Current weather stations require manual data collection, becoming unmanageable with multiple units. There is no centralized system for real-time data or analytics, and third-party platforms are costly and overly complex.
The Solution The platform uses AWS IoT Core to ingest MQTT data, AWS Lambda and API Gateway for processing, Amazon S3 for storage (including a data lake), and AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to extract, transform, and load data from the S3 data lake to another S3 bucket for analysis. AWS Amplify with Next.js provides the web interface, and Amazon Cognito ensures secure access. Similar to Thingsboard and CoreIoT, users can register new devices and manage connections, though this platform operates on a smaller scale and is designed for private use. Key features include real-time dashboards, trend analysis, and low operational costs.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution establishes a foundational resource for lab members to develop a larger IoT platform, serving as a study resource, and provides a data foundation for AI enthusiasts for model training or analysis. It reduces manual reporting for each station via a centralized platform, simplifying management and maintenance, and improves data reliability. Monthly costs are $0.66 USD per the AWS Pricing Calculator, with a 12-month total of $7.92 USD. All IoT equipment costs are covered by the existing weather station setup, eliminating additional development expenses. The break-even period of 6-12 months is achieved through significant time savings from reduced manual work.
3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. title: Saga with Step Functions: how do you roll back an order when payment fails?
content:
This comes up a lot when moving from a monolith to microservices.
Creating the order, taking stock and recording the payment used to live in one database. BEGIN TRANSACTION … COMMIT was enough, and any error meant ROLLBACK for everything.
After splitting into services, each part has its own database:
The Orders service writes the order to the Orders table. The Inventory service reserves stock in the Inventory table. The Payment service calls an external payment gateway. One day, order #1042 is created and the stock is reserved, but the payment fails because the card is declined. The order is stuck in PENDING, and the last item in stock is “locked” for an order that will never complete.
There’s no shared transaction to ROLLBACK anymore. So how does the system undo its own work?
1. Why can’t we use a transaction like before? A relational database guarantees ACID within one database. When data spans several databases owned by several services, the traditional answer is two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator asks every participant to “promise” to commit, and only then commits for real.
AWS Prescriptive Guidance points out that with database-per-service, 2PC isn’t an option, because there’s no shared coordinator across different data stores [1]. On top of that, an external payment gateway won’t take part in your transaction anyway.
The common answer is the Saga pattern: split the big transaction into a chain of small steps, each one a local transaction in its own service. For every step, prepare a compensating transaction that “undoes it in business terms” if something fails later.
2. Orchestration: let Step Functions conduct There are two ways to run a saga:
Choreography: services publish and listen to each other’s events. Orchestration: a central orchestrator knows every step and decides what runs next. AWS suggests an AWS Step Functions Standard Workflow as the orchestrator [1]. For the order example:
Success path:
T1 Create order (PENDING) → T2 Reserve stock (RESERVED) → T3 Charge payment (PAID) → CONFIRMED Compensation path, running backwards:
Failure at T1 → Fail, nothing to undo yet. Failure at T2 → C2 Release stock (if it was reserved) → C1 Cancel order → Fail. Failure at T3 → C3 Refund (if money was taken) → C2 Release stock → C1 Cancel order → Fail. The rule: compensate in reverse order, and each compensating step checks for itself whether there’s anything to undo.
Why Standard and not Express? Standard Workflows run exactly-once (unless you configure Retry), keep execution history and can run for up to a year, which suits non-idempotent work like payments. Express Workflows are at-least-once (async) or at-most-once (sync) and run for five minutes at most [3].
Also, if you set the execution name to the orderId, a Standard Workflow won’t start a new execution with the same name while the old one is still running [3]. That’s one layer of protection against duplicate sagas when a customer clicks “Place order” twice.
3. Retry and Catch for two different kinds of error Not every error needs a rollback. Step Functions gives a Task state two tools [2]:
Retry, for temporary errors: timeouts, throttling, 5xx from the payment gateway.
"Retry": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["Payment.Timeout", "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException"], "IntervalSeconds": 2, "MaxAttempts": 3, "BackoffRate": 2, "JitterStrategy": "FULL" }] Catch, for business errors or when retries run out: a declined card, out of stock.
"Catch": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["CardDeclined"], "ResultPath": "$.error", "Next": "RefundPayment" }, { "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "ResultPath": "$.error", "Next": "RefundPayment" }] A few details worth knowing [2]:
When a state has both Retry and Catch, Step Functions retries first and only moves to Catch if retrying doesn’t fix it. The defaults are MaxAttempts = 3 and BackoffRate = 2.0. JitterStrategy: FULL keeps retries from all landing at the same moment. States.ALL has to be alone in ErrorEquals and sit in the last catcher. Without a ResultPath, the error output replaces the whole input. Set ResultPath: "$.error" to keep orderId, paymentId and so on for the compensating steps. 4. Retry can run the payment step twice Say the Lambda calls the payment gateway, the gateway takes the money, but the response times out. Step Functions sees an error and retries T3. Without any safeguard, the customer is charged twice.
Standard Workflow’s exactly-once only promises that a state won’t run again outside your Retry settings [3]. Once you turn Retry on, you’ve allowed T3 to run again yourself.
That’s why AWS stresses that saga participants must be idempotent so they can safely run again after temporary errors [1]. In the example:
T3 sends Idempotency-Key = orderId (if the payment gateway supports it). T2 reserves stock with a conditional write keyed on orderId, so repeated calls don’t take more stock. T1 creates the order with PutItem and an attribute_not_exists condition. 5. Compensating steps can fail too A refund is also a call to an external API, so it can time out too.
A few rules for compensating transactions:
Idempotent: refunding twice must not pay the money back twice. Before refunding, check whether the charge happened and whether it was already refunded. Handle “nothing to undo”: if T3 failed before charging, C3 checks the status and skips. Retry longer than normal steps: a failed compensation means your data is inconsistent right now. Never fail silently: when retries run out, Catch into a state that sends to Amazon SNS or raises an alarm so the ops team can fix it by hand. 6. A saga has no isolation While a saga is running, data across the services is “half done”: the order exists but isn’t paid, the stock is reserved but not sold.
AWS notes that sagas lack transaction isolation and recommends a semantic lock [1]. A simple way is to use the order status as a business lock:
PENDING → RESERVED → PAID → CONFIRMED (failure at any step) → CANCELLED Other parts of the system (shipping, confirmation emails, revenue reports) only act on orders that are CONFIRMED. Orders in PENDING or RESERVED aren’t final yet.
A saga also gives you eventual consistency, not strong consistency. Agree with the business side that for a short time the stock shown may not match exactly [1].
7. Checklist before a saga goes to production Does every step T have a matching compensating step C, run in reverse order? Are temporary errors (Retry) kept apart from business errors (Catch)? Does Catch use ResultPath to keep the data the compensating steps need? Are all T and C steps idempotent, even when retried? Does a failed compensating step raise an alarm, with a manual process to fix it? Do other systems only read orders that are final? Is logging/X-Ray on for the state machine so each saga can be traced? Conclusion Once you move to microservices, rolling back has to be designed into the business flow as compensating steps.
Saga orchestration with Step Functions puts the whole success path and compensation path in one place you can see, retry and trace. But Step Functions only coordinates. Correctness still lives in each service: every step has to be safe to run again, and every compensating step has to handle the case where there’s nothing to undo.
A saga needs Retry for temporary errors, Catch for business errors and idempotency in every step. Without all three, the saga itself can leave the data inconsistent.
References AWS Prescriptive Guidance: Saga orchestration pattern Handling errors in Step Functions workflows Choosing workflow type in Step Functions FCAJ Workshop: Workflow Orchestration with AWS Step Functions

Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from VPCs and your on-premises networks, without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this lab, you will learn how to create, configure, and test VPC endpoints that enable your workloads to reach AWS services without traversing the Public Internet.
You will create two types of endpoints to access Amazon S3: a Gateway VPC endpoint, and an Interface VPC endpoint. These two types of VPC endpoints offer different benefits depending on if you are accessing Amazon S3 from the cloud or your on-premises location
Gateway - Create a gateway endpoint to send traffic to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB using private IP addresses.You route traffic from your VPC to the gateway endpoint using route tables. Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS.
